readings.title: First reading
readings.text:
The path of the upright man is straight,
you smooth the way of the upright.
Following the path of your judgements,
we hoped in you, O Lord,
your name, your memory are all my soul desires.
At night my soul longs for you
and my spirit in me seeks for you;
when your judgements appear on earth
the inhabitants of the world learn the meaning of integrity.
O Lord, you are giving us peace,
since you treat us
as our deeds deserve.
Distressed, we search for you, O Lord;
the misery of oppression was your punishment for us.
As a woman with child near her time
writhes and cries out in her pangs,
so are we, O Lord, in your presence:
we have conceived, we writhe
as if we were giving birth;
we have not given the spirit of salvation to the earth,
no more inhabitants of the world are born.
Your dead will come to life,
their corpses will rise;
awake, exult,
all you who lie in the dust,
for your dew is a radiant dew
and the land of ghosts will give birth.

exegesis.summary: Isaiah portrays the just soul yearning for God in the night, acknowledging that peace is God's gift and that Israel's own labors have failed to bring forth salvation. Yet the prophet erupts in a startling hope: the dead will live, corpses shall rise, and the dust will yield its inhabitants at the touch of the Lord's radiant dew. This is one of the Old Testament's clearest anticipations of the resurrection of the body.

patristicQuotes.quote: In the end of the world all that are in their graves shall hear His voice, and come forth. They that have done good shall go unto the resurrection of life, that is, to live with the Angels of God; they that have done evil unto the resurrection of judgment.
He who rests secure concerning his hope and works, immediately opens to Him that knocks; for when he is aware of the time of death drawing near, he grows joyful, because of the glory of his reward.

cccReferences.title: The heart restless until it rests in God
Resurrection of the just and the unjust
Illness, conversion, and the God who heals

exegesis.thematicConnection: Isaiah's cry — 'at night my soul longs for you' — is the very labor and heavy burden that Christ answers in the Gospel with 'Come to me.' The promise that the dust will rise anticipates Christ, who alone gives rest to souls and life to the dead.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
The Lord looked down from heaven to the earth.
You, O Lord, will endure for ever
and your name from age to age.
You will arise and have mercy on Zion:
for this is the time to have mercy,
for your servants love her very stones,
are moved with pity even for her dust.
The Lord looked down from heaven to the earth.
The nations shall fear the name of the Lord
and all the earth’s kings your glory,
when the Lord shall build up Zion again
and appear in all his glory.
Then he will turn to the prayers of the helpless;
he will not despise their prayers.
The Lord looked down from heaven to the earth.
Let this be written for ages to come
that a people yet unborn may praise the Lord;
for the Lord leaned down from his sanctuary on high.
He looked down from heaven to the earth
that he might hear the groans of the prisoners
and free those condemned to die.
The Lord looked down from heaven to the earth.
readings.refrain: The Lord looked down from heaven to the earth.

exegesis.summary: The psalmist sings of the Lord who leans down from His holy heights to hear the groans of prisoners and to free those condemned to die. The Lord is enthroned forever, yet He stoops in mercy to rebuild Zion and to answer the prayer of the destitute. This is written 'for a people yet unborn,' making the psalm a bridge between the promises of Isaiah and their fulfillment in Christ.

patristicQuotes.quote: The Lord sees them, and has compassion upon them, and heals all sickness and infirmity, that is, He cleanses their obstructed minds and unbelieving hearts for the understanding of the new preaching.

cccReferences.title: Prayer in the shadow of God's dwelling
The Father answers by raising His Son
Christ descends to free those in death's bondage

exegesis.thematicConnection: The Lord who 'looks down from heaven' to hear the prisoners' groans is the same Lord who, in Matthew, calls all who labor and are burdened to Himself. Both readings envision God bending down to the weary — Isaiah's dead in the dust, the psalmist's condemned prisoners, the Gospel's overburdened.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text: Jesus said, ‘Come to me, all you who labour and are overburdened, and I will give you rest. Shoulder my yoke and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. Yes, my yoke is easy and my burden light.’

exegesis.summary: In one of the tenderest passages of all Scripture, Jesus invites the weary of the world to come to Him and receive rest. He offers His yoke — the Gospel and its commandments — which is not a new bondage but a lightening of the crushing weight of sin. He gives Himself as the model of the meek and humble heart, the true Teacher from whom the disciple learns rest.

patristicQuotes.quote: In beginning the Divine Law He begins with humility, and sets before us a great reward: 'ye shall find rest for your souls.' This is the highest reward — you shall not only be made useful to others, but shall make yourself to have peace.

What is more pleasant than that yoke, what lighter than that burden? To be made better, to abstain from wickedness, to choose the good and refuse the evil, to love all men, to hate none, to gain eternal things.
The yoke of Christ is Christ's Gospel, which joins and yokes together Jews and Gentiles in the unity of the faith. This we are commanded to take upon us, that is, to have in honor.

cccReferences.title: Take my yoke — Christ our model of holiness

exegesis.thematicConnection: Christ answers directly the anguish of Isaiah's 'we writhe as if in labor' and the psalmist's 'groans of the prisoners.' The rest Jesus promises is the very salvation Isaiah could not bring forth — the resurrection life given to souls yoked to the meek and humble Lord.

synthesis.title: Come to the God who bends down and raises the dust to life
synthesis.body: Today the Church places before us the whole arc of the soul's longing and God's response. Isaiah gives voice to a people writhing in labor pains, unable to bring forth salvation from themselves, yet daring to believe that the Lord's radiant dew will awaken the dust and raise the dead. The Psalmist sees this same Lord not as a distant king but as One who leans down from His holy height to hear the groans of prisoners and free those condemned to die. And then, in the Gospel, the God who bends down speaks in the human voice of Jesus: 'Come to me, all you who labor and are overburdened.' The rest that Israel could not conceive, that the prisoner could only groan for, Christ simply gives — to those who take His yoke, which is the Gospel and the imitation of His meek and humble Heart. As St. John Chrysostom teaches, Christ begins His Law with humility because humility alone opens us to receive the rest of God. We were made, the Catechism reminds us, for Him — and our hearts are restless until they rest in Him. Today, then, is an invitation: lay down the impossible burden of self-salvation, and let the Lord who raises the dead raise you too.
